Lecture 33

Laplace’s equation and plane boundary-value problems

We prove Green’s first identity on a region of GM 40 and use it to show that the Dirichlet problem has at most one solution and that the Neumann problem needs a compatibility condition. We prove the maximum principle, solve rectangular problems by separation of variables, and examine what corner data do to a solution.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Interpret Laplace’s and Poisson’s equations in steady heat flow, electrostatics, potential flow and gravitation, and state the boundary data each problem takes.
  • Prove uniqueness for the Dirichlet problem on a rectangle by the energy argument and by the maximum principle, and check the compatibility condition of a Neumann problem.
  • Choose sine, cosine and hyperbolic factors from the boundary conditions and solve a rectangular problem as a series, with its convergence for Dirichlet data.
  • Explain what goes wrong when edge data disagree at a corner.

A string held at rest and a rod whose temperature no longer changes are in equilibrium. In two and three dimensions an equilibrium field solves Laplace’s equation ∇2u=0\laplacian u=0∇2u=0, or Poisson’s equation ∇2u=−f\laplacian u=-f∇2u=−f when sources are present. Lecture 29 explained that such an equation takes one condition on the whole boundary of its region, not Cauchy data. In this lecture we prove that this condition determines the solution, and we construct solutions on a rectangle with the sine series of Lecture 32. The lecture reads in four stages: equilibrium fields and uniqueness (Sections 33.1–33.2), separation of variables on a rectangle (Section 33.3), corners (Section 33.4), and Neumann problems and the choice of factors (Sections 33.5–33.6).

33.1 Equilibrium fields

Throughout the lecture the unknown uuu is a real function of a position x\vv xx in an open set U⊂R2U\subset\R^2U⊂R2 or U⊂R3U\subset\R^3U⊂R3, and ∇2u=uxx+uyy\laplacian u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}∇2u=uxx​+uyy​ in the plane.

Definition 33.1 (Harmonic function and Poisson equation). A real function uuu with continuous second partial derivatives on UUU is harmonic on UUU if ∇2u=0on U.\laplacian u=0\quad\text{on }U .∇2u=0on U.(33.1) For a continuous function fff on UUU, the Poisson equation is ∇2u=−fon U.\laplacian u=-f\quad\text{on }U .∇2u=−fon U.(33.2)

The definition of a harmonic function is that of Lectures 2 and 15, with the examples ln⁡r\ln rlnr off the origin of the plane (Lecture 2), 1/r1/r1/r off the origin of space (Lecture 3), x2−y2x^2-y^2x2−y2 and xyxyxy (Lecture 15). The same two equations describe several equilibria.

  • Steady heat flow. A temperature that does not change in time solves Lecture 29’s heat equation with ut=0u_t=0ut​=0, so Poisson’s equation holds with fff equal to the heat source density divided by the conductivity κ\kappaκ. An insulated boundary has no heat flux through it, so the derivative of uuu along the outward normal vanishes there.

  • Electrostatics. The electric potential uuu gives the field −∇u-\grad u−∇u, and fff is the charge density divided by the vacuum permittivity (Lecture 29). A conductor held at a prescribed potential supplies Dirichlet data.

  • Potential flow. An incompressible, irrotational flow with a velocity potential uuu has the velocity ∇u\grad u∇u and ∇2u=0\laplacian u=0∇2u=0 (Lecture 29). Fluid does not cross a fixed wall, so the normal component of ∇u\grad u∇u vanishes on the wall.

  • Gravitation. The Newtonian potential uuu of a mass density ρm\rho_{\mathrm m}ρm​ satisfies ∇2u=4πGρm\laplacian u=4\pi G\rho_{\mathrm m}∇2u=4πGρm​, with the gravitational constant GGG, and is harmonic where there is no mass. Its usual condition is at infinity, which this lecture does not treat.

  • Quantum mechanics. For a free particle with the energy zero the time-independent Schrödinger equation is −(ℏ2/2m)∇2u=0-(\hbar^2/2m)\laplacian u=0−(ℏ2/2m)∇2u=0 (Lecture 29’s table). A particle confined to a rectangle has u=0u=0u=0 on its edges, and with these data Laplace’s equation has only the solution u=0u=0u=0 (Section 33.2, applied to the real and imaginary parts). So a confined particle has no state of energy zero. Its states of positive energy solve the Helmholtz equation of Lecture 41.

The data of these equations live on the boundary of the region. For an open set UUU in the plane, a point p\vv pp is a boundary point of UUU if every ball about p\vv pp contains points of UUU and points outside UUU. The set of boundary points is the boundary ∂U\partial U∂U, and U‾=U∪∂U\overline U=U\cup\partial UU=U∪∂U is the closure of UUU. We work mostly on the open rectangle R=(0,Lx)×(0,Ly),Lx>0, Ly>0,R=(0,L_x)\times(0,L_y),\qquad L_x>0,\ L_y>0,R=(0,Lx​)×(0,Ly​),Lx​>0, Ly​>0,(33.3) whose closure R‾=[0,Lx]×[0,Ly]\overline R=[0,L_x]\times[0,L_y]R=[0,Lx​]×[0,Ly​] is a closed box in the sense of Lecture 29 and whose boundary ∂R\partial R∂R consists of its four edges. On an edge the outward unit normal n\vv nn points out of RRR, and the outward normal derivative is ∂nu=∇u⋅n\partial_nu=\grad u\cdot\vv n∂n​u=∇u⋅n, as in GM 42. On the bottom edge y=0y=0y=0, for example, n=(0,−1)\vv n=(0,-1)n=(0,−1) and ∂nu=−uy\partial_nu=-u_y∂n​u=−uy​. At the four corners n\vv nn is not defined.

R=(0,Lx)×(0,Ly),Lx>0, Ly>0,R=(0,L_x)\times(0,L_y),\qquad L_x>0,\ L_y>0,R=(0,Lx​)×(0,Ly​),Lx​>0, Ly​>0,(33.3)

Definition 33.2 (Dirichlet and Neumann problems). Let UUU be a bounded open set in the plane, fff continuous on UUU and ggg a given function on ∂U\partial U∂U.

  • A solution of the Dirichlet problem is a function u∈C2(U)u\in C^2(U)u∈C2(U) that is continuous on U‾\overline UU and satisfies ∇2u=−f\laplacian u=-f∇2u=−f on UUU and u=gu=gu=g on ∂U\partial U∂U.

  • For U=RU=RU=R, a solution of the Neumann problem is a function u∈C2(R)u\in C^2(R)u∈C2(R) that is continuous on R‾\overline RR, whose first partial derivatives extend continuously to R‾\overline RR, and that satisfies ∇2u=−f\laplacian u=-f∇2u=−f on RRR and ∂nu=g\partial_nu=g∂n​u=g on ∂R\partial R∂R except at the corners.

In the examples above, a held temperature and a conductor held at a prescribed potential give Dirichlet data, while an insulated boundary, a prescribed heat flux and a wall give Neumann data.

33.2 Green’s identity, uniqueness and the maximum principle

For the string, Lecture 31 proved uniqueness from the conservation of energy. For an equilibrium the corresponding quantity is the integral of ∣∇u∣2\abs{\grad u}^2∣∇u∣2, and the tool that controls it is an integration by parts in two variables. GM 40 proves Green’s theorem ∮∂DP ⁣dx+Q ⁣dy=∬D(∂xQ−∂yP) ⁣dA\oint_{\partial D}P\dd x+Q\dd y=\iint_D(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\dd A∮∂D​Pdx+Qdy=∬D​(∂x​Q−∂y​P)dA for a compact region DDD (written as in GM 40; it is not the diffusivity DDD of Lecture 29) that is simple in both coordinate directions, with positively oriented boundary, and for PPP and QQQ continuously differentiable on an open set containing DDD. Such a region lies between two graphs over the xxx-axis and between two graphs over the yyy-axis. A closed rectangle is such a region.

Lemma 33.3 (Green’s first identity). Let DDD be a compact region as in GM 40’s Green theorem, with outward unit normal n\vv nn on ∂D\partial D∂D (except at finitely many corners) and arc length  ⁣ds\dd sds. Let www be continuously differentiable and uuu twice continuously differentiable on an open set containing DDD. Then ∬D(w∇2u+∇w⋅∇u) ⁣dA=∮∂Dw ∂nu ⁣ds.\iint_D\bigl(w\laplacian u+\grad w\cdot\grad u\bigr)\dd A=\oint_{\partial D}w\,\partial_nu\dd s .∬D​(w∇2u+∇w⋅∇u)dA=∮∂D​w∂n​uds.(33.4)

Proof. We apply Green’s theorem with P=−wuyP=-wu_yP=−wuy​ and Q=wuxQ=wu_xQ=wux​, which are continuously differentiable. Then ∂xQ−∂yP=wxux+wuxx+wyuy+wuyy=∇w⋅∇u+w∇2u.\partial_xQ-\partial_yP=w_xu_x+wu_{xx}+w_yu_y+wu_{yy}=\grad w\cdot\grad u+w\laplacian u .∂x​Q−∂y​P=wx​ux​+wuxx​+wy​uy​+wuyy​=∇w⋅∇u+w∇2u. On the boundary, let (x(s),y(s))(x(s),y(s))(x(s),y(s)) run along ∂D\partial D∂D in the positive direction with unit speed, so that (x′,y′)(x',y')(x′,y′) is the unit tangent. The region lies on the left of the tangent, so the outward normal is the tangent turned clockwise by a right angle, n=(y′,−x′)\vv n=(y',-x')n=(y′,−x′). Hence P ⁣dx+Q ⁣dy=w(uxy′−uyx′) ⁣ds=w ∇u⋅n ⁣ds=w ∂nu ⁣ds,P\dd x+Q\dd y=w\bigl(u_xy'-u_yx'\bigr)\dd s=w\,\grad u\cdot\vv n\dd s=w\,\partial_nu\dd s,Pdx+Qdy=w(ux​y′−uy​x′)ds=w∇u⋅nds=w∂n​uds, and Green’s theorem gives (33.4). ■

With w=1w=1w=1 the identity gives ∬D∇2u ⁣dA=∮∂D∂nu ⁣ds\iint_D\laplacian u\dd A=\oint_{\partial D}\partial_nu\dd s∬D​∇2udA=∮∂D​∂n​uds, the plane form of a consequence of Gauss’s theorem in GM 42. With w=uw=uw=u and ∇2u=0\laplacian u=0∇2u=0 it gives ∬D∣∇u∣2 ⁣dA=∮∂Du ∂nu ⁣ds.\iint_D\abs{\grad u}^2\dd A=\oint_{\partial D}u\,\partial_nu\dd s .∬D​∣∇u∣2dA=∮∂D​u∂n​uds.(33.5) The left side is the analogue of the energy of Lecture 31. It vanishes only for a constant uuu, and this is the idea of the next theorem. The solutions of the definition need not be differentiable on an open set containing R‾\overline RR, so we apply the identity on slightly smaller rectangles and pass to the limit.

∬D∣∇u∣2 ⁣dA=∮∂Du ∂nu ⁣ds.\iint_D\abs{\grad u}^2\dd A=\oint_{\partial D}u\,\partial_nu\dd s .∬D​∣∇u∣2dA=∮∂D​u∂n​uds.(33.5)

Theorem 33.4 (Uniqueness by energy). Let u1u_1u1​ and u2u_2u2​ be twice continuously differentiable on RRR, with u1u_1u1​, u2u_2u2​ and their first partial derivatives continuous on R‾\overline RR, and let ∇2u1=∇2u2\laplacian u_1=\laplacian u_2∇2u1​=∇2u2​ on RRR.

In particular the Dirichlet problem has at most one solution whose first derivatives are continuous on R‾\overline RR, and the Neumann problem has at most one solution up to an additive constant.

Proof. The difference w=u1−u2w=u_1-u_2w=u1​−u2​ is harmonic on RRR, and www, wxw_xwx​ and wyw_ywy​ are continuous on R‾\overline RR. In both cases w ∂nw=0w\,\partial_nw=0w∂n​w=0 on ∂R\partial R∂R except at the corners.

First, for 0<δ<12min⁡(Lx,Ly)0<\delta<\tfrac12\min(L_x,L_y)0<δ<21​min(Lx​,Ly​) let Rδ=[δ,Lx−δ]×[δ,Ly−δ]R_\delta=[\delta,L_x-\delta]\times[\delta,L_y-\delta]Rδ​=[δ,Lx​−δ]×[δ,Ly​−δ]. The function www is twice continuously differentiable on the open set RRR, which contains RδR_\deltaRδ​, so (33.5) holds on RδR_\deltaRδ​: ∬Rδ∣∇w∣2 ⁣dA=∮∂Rδw ∂nw ⁣ds.\iint_{R_\delta}\abs{\grad w}^2\dd A=\oint_{\partial R_\delta}w\,\partial_nw\dd s .∬Rδ​​∣∇w∣2dA=∮∂Rδ​​w∂n​wds. Next, we let δ→0+\delta\to0^+δ→0+. The functions w wxw\,w_xwwx​ and w wyw\,w_ywwy​ are continuous on the closed box R‾\overline RR, hence uniformly continuous there, by Lecture 29’s lemma on continuous functions on closed boxes. On the bottom edge of RδR_\deltaRδ​ the integrand is −w(x,δ)wy(x,δ)-w(x,\delta)w_y(x,\delta)−w(x,δ)wy​(x,δ), which therefore tends to −w(x,0)wy(x,0)=0-w(x,0)w_y(x,0)=0−w(x,0)wy​(x,0)=0 uniformly in xxx. The bottom edge of RδR_\deltaRδ​ is shorter than LxL_xLx​, so the integral over it tends to 000. The other three edges behave in the same way. Hence the right side tends to 000. On the left, ∣∇w∣2\abs{\grad w}^2∣∇w∣2 is continuous and bounded on R‾\overline RR, and R∖RδR\setminus R_\deltaR∖Rδ​ has an area at most 2δ(Lx+Ly)2\delta(L_x+L_y)2δ(Lx​+Ly​), so the left side tends to ∬R∣∇w∣2 ⁣dA\iint_R\abs{\grad w}^2\dd A∬R​∣∇w∣2dA. Applied with w=1w=1w=1, Green’s identity also gives a condition that the data of a Neumann problem must satisfy.

Proposition 33.5 (Neumann compatibility). If the Neumann problem on RRR with a source fff continuous on R‾\overline RR and data ggg has a solution, then ∮∂Rg ⁣ds=−∬Rf ⁣dA.\oint_{\partial R}g\dd s=-\iint_Rf\dd A .∮∂R​gds=−∬R​fdA.(33.6)

The left side is −∬Rδf ⁣dA-\iint_{R_\delta}f\dd A−∬Rδ​​fdA, which tends to −∬Rf ⁣dA-\iint_Rf\dd A−∬R​fdA as δ→0+\delta\to0^+δ→0+ because fff is bounded on R‾\overline RR. The first derivatives of uuu are uniformly continuous on R‾\overline RR, so, as in the previous proof, the integral over each edge of RδR_\deltaRδ​ tends to the integral over the matching part of ∂R\partial R∂R. The parts of ∂R\partial R∂R that RδR_\deltaRδ​ misses near the corners have the total length 8δ8\delta8δ, and they contribute at most 8δmax⁡R‾∣∇u∣8\delta\max_{\overline R}\abs{\grad u}8δmaxR​∣∇u∣. So the right side tends to ∮∂R∂nu ⁣ds=∮∂Rg ⁣ds\oint_{\partial R}\partial_nu\dd s=\oint_{\partial R}g\dd s∮∂R​∂n​uds=∮∂R​gds. ■

In steady heat flow the condition says that the heat leaving through the boundary equals the heat produced inside. Indeed, −κ ∂nu-\kappa\,\partial_nu−κ∂n​u is the outward heat flux density, and (33.6) multiplied by −κ-\kappa−κ reads “total outward flux === total production”. If a plate with insulated edges is heated inside, there is no steady state. Lecture 37 shows the same growth of the temperature for a rod with insulated ends and a heat source.

The solutions constructed below are continuous on R‾\overline RR, but their first derivatives need not be. If the top data ggg have a kink at x0x_0x0​, then uxu_xux​ has no continuous extension to (x0,Ly)(x_0,L_y)(x0​,Ly​), since on the top edge it would equal g′g'g′. For these solutions we need uniqueness in the larger class of Definition 33.2. It comes from the maximum principle, which says that a steady temperature without sources is nowhere hotter than the hottest point of the boundary.

For Laplace’s equation with data on ∂R\partial R∂R that are continuous on ∂R\partial R∂R and piecewise C1C^1C1 on each edge, Section 33.4 proves existence. So this problem is well posed in the sense of Lecture 29, with the size of data and solutions measured by the maximum of the absolute value, unlike the Cauchy problem of Hadamard’s example.

33.3 Separation of variables on a rectangle

We now construct solutions. We first take the simplest data: a temperature or potential that is zero on three edges of the rectangle and given on the top edge, ∇2u=0 on R,u(x,0)=0,u(0,y)=0,u(Lx,y)=0,u(x,Ly)=g(x),\laplacian u=0\ \text{on }R,\qquad u(x,0)=0,\quad u(0,y)=0,\quad u(L_x,y)=0,\quad u(x,L_y)=g(x),∇2u=0 on R,u(x,0)=0,u(0,y)=0,u(Lx​,y)=0,u(x,Ly​)=g(x),(33.7) as in Figure 33.1. A solution continuous on R‾\overline RR has the value 000 at the top corners, which belong to the side edges as well. So we assume g(0)=g(Lx)=0.g(0)=g(L_x)=0 .g(0)=g(Lx​)=0.(33.8)

Separated solutions. We look for solutions of the form u=X(x)Y(y)u=X(x)Y(y)u=X(x)Y(y), with letters local to this lecture. The left side depends only on xxx and the right side only on yyy, so both equal a constant (by the argument of Lecture 32, at points where XY≠0XY\ne0XY=0), which we write −λ-\lambda−λ: −X′′=λX,Y′′=λY.-X''=\lambda X,\qquad Y''=\lambda Y .−X′′=λX,Y′′=λY. The conditions on the side edges require X(0)=X(Lx)=0X(0)=X(L_x)=0X(0)=X(Lx​)=0. Lecture 32 solved this eigenvalue problem: it has nonzero solutions exactly for λ=kn2\lambda=k_n^2λ=kn2​ with kn=nπ/Lxk_n=n\pi/L_xkn​=nπ/Lx​, n=1,2,…n=1,2,\ldotsn=1,2,…, and they are the multiples of sin⁡(knx)\sin(k_nx)sin(kn​x). For λ=kn2\lambda=k_n^2λ=kn2​ the condition on the bottom edge requires Y(0)=0Y(0)=0Y(0)=0, and the solutions of Y′′=kn2YY''=k_n^2YY′′=kn2​Y with Y(0)=0Y(0)=0Y(0)=0 are the multiples of sinh⁡(kny)\sinh(k_ny)sinh(kn​y). 33.4 Data on all four edges and discontinuous corners

A Dirichlet problem usually prescribes data on all four edges. Let gbg_{\mathrm b}gb​, gtg_{\mathrm t}gt​, glg_{\mathrm l}gl​ and grg_{\mathrm r}gr​ be the data on the bottom, top, left and right edges, each continuous and piecewise C1C^1C1. A solution continuous on R‾\overline RR needs the data to agree at the corners, for example gb(0)=gl(0)g_{\mathrm b}(0)=g_{\mathrm l}(0)gb​(0)=gl​(0) at the corner (0,0)(0,0)(0,0).

If all four data vanish at both ends of their edges, the problem splits into four problems of the form (33.7). The problem with data on the bottom edge is solved by (33.10) with yyy replaced by Ly−yL_y-yLy​−y, that is, with the factor sinh⁡(kn(Ly−y))/sinh⁡(knLy)\sinh(k_n(L_y-y))/\sinh(k_nL_y)sinh(kn​(Ly​−y))/sinh(kn​Ly​). The problems with data on the side edges are solved in the same way with the roles of xxx and yyy exchanged, with the sine series in yyy on (0,Ly)(0,L_y)(0,Ly​) and the wave numbers μn=nπ/Ly\mu_n=n\pi/L_yμn​=nπ/Ly​. For the right edge, u(x,y)=∑n=1∞bnr sinh⁡(μnx)sinh⁡(μnLx) sin⁡(μny),bnr=2Ly∫0Lygr(y)sin⁡(μny) ⁣dy,u(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n^{\mathrm r}\,\frac{\sinh(\mu_nx)}{\sinh(\mu_nL_x)}\,\sin(\mu_ny),\qquad b_n^{\mathrm r}=\frac2{L_y}\int_0^{L_y}g_{\mathrm r}(y)\sin(\mu_ny)\dd y ,u(x,y)=n=1∑∞​bnr​sinh(μn​Lx​)sinh(μn​x)​sin(μn​y),bnr​=Ly​2​∫0Ly​​gr​(y)sin(μn​y)dy, and for the left edge sinh⁡(μnx)\sinh(\mu_nx)sinh(μn​x) is replaced by sinh⁡(μn(Lx−x))\sinh(\mu_n(L_x-x))sinh(μn​(Lx​−x)) and grg_{\mathrm r}gr​ by glg_{\mathrm l}gl​. The sum of the four solutions is harmonic, continuous on R‾\overline RR and has the prescribed data on every edge.

If the data are continuous on ∂R\partial R∂R but do not vanish at the corners, we first remove the corner values. The four functions 111, xxx, yyy and xyxyxy are harmonic, and so is every combination B(x,y)=β0+β1x+β2y+β3xy.B(x,y)=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2y+\beta_3xy .B(x,y)=β0​+β1​x+β2​y+β3​xy. Its four coefficients can be chosen so that BBB takes the four prescribed corner values: the values at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), (Lx,0)(L_x,0)(Lx​,0) and (0,Ly)(0,L_y)(0,Ly​) fix β0\beta_0β0​, β1\beta_1β1​ and β2\beta_2β2​, and the value at (Lx,Ly)(L_x,L_y)(Lx​,Ly​) then fixes β3\beta_3β3​. On each edge BBB is a linear function. The data minus the values of BBB vanish at the corners, and the solution is BBB plus the solution for these reduced data. Together with Theorem 33.9, this solves the Dirichlet problem for Laplace’s equation on RRR for all data on ∂R\partial R∂R that are continuous on ∂R\partial R∂R and piecewise C1C^1C1 on each edge.

When the data disagree at a corner, no solution is continuous on R‾\overline RR, and the uniqueness theorems above do not apply. The simplest example is a constant on one edge.

The solution of Example 33.11 is not covered by Proposition 33.7, because it is not continuous on R‾\overline RR. This lecture does not prove such a theorem, and nothing in it depends on it.

33.5 Neumann problems on a rectangle

33.6 Choosing the factors

The method of Sections 33.3 and 33.5 consists of the following steps.

  • Find the direction in which the conditions on both opposite edges are homogeneous, say xxx.

  • Solve −X′′=λX-X''=\lambda X−X′′=λX with these conditions (Table 33.1).

  • Choose the factor sinh⁡\sinhsinh or cosh⁡\coshcosh in the other direction from its homogeneous edge.

  • Expand the data on the remaining edge in the eigenfunctions XnX_nXn​, and divide each coefficient by the value of the factor (Dirichlet data) or of its derivative (Neumann data) on that edge.

Data on several edges are split by superposition, as in Section 33.4. With Neumann data on every edge, each piece must satisfy its own compatibility condition, a case this lecture does not treat. Table 33.1 lists the four cases on (0,Lx)(0,L_x)(0,Lx​).

Summary

Laplace’s and Poisson’s equations describe equilibria. A Dirichlet problem prescribes uuu on the boundary, a Neumann problem its outward normal derivative. Green’s first identity gives uniqueness for solutions with first derivatives continuous up to the boundary and the compatibility condition of the Neumann problem. The maximum principle gives uniqueness and continuous dependence for solutions that are only continuous up to the boundary. On a rectangle, separation of variables gives sine series times hyperbolic factors. A constant edge, whose data jump at two corners, gives a bounded harmonic function that is not continuous there.

  • Green’s first identity: ∬D(w∇2u+∇w⋅∇u) ⁣dA=∮∂Dw ∂nu ⁣ds\iint_D(w\laplacian u+\grad w\cdot\grad u)\dd A=\oint_{\partial D}w\,\partial_nu\dd s∬D​(w∇2u+∇w⋅∇u)dA=∮∂D​w∂n​uds on a region DDD of GM 40.

  • Uniqueness by energy: for solutions with first derivatives continuous on R‾\overline RR, Dirichlet data determine uuu, Neumann data determine uuu up to a constant.

  • Neumann compatibility: necessary for a solution, ∮∂Rg ⁣ds=−∬Rf ⁣dA\oint_{\partial R}g\dd s=-\iint_Rf\dd A∮∂R​gds=−∬R​fdA.

  • Maximum principle: a harmonic uuu continuous on R‾\overline RR takes its maximum and minimum on ∂R\partial R∂R, so max⁡∣u1−u2∣≤max⁡∂R∣g1−g2∣\max\abs{u_1-u_2}\le\max_{\partial R}\abs{g_1-g_2}max∣u1​−u2​∣≤max∂R​∣g1​−g2​∣ for two Dirichlet solutions with the same source.

  • One edge: u=∑bnsinh⁡(kny)sin⁡(knx)/sinh⁡(knLy)u=\sum b_n\sinh(k_ny)\sin(k_nx)/\sinh(k_nL_y)u=∑bn​sinh(kn​y)sin(kn​x)/sinh(kn​Ly​) for continuous, piecewise C1C^1C1 data ggg with g(0)=g(Lx)=0g(0)=g(L_x)=0g(0)=g(Lx​)=0.

  • Corners: β0+β1x+β2y+β3xy\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2y+\beta_3xyβ0​+β1​x+β2​y+β3​xy removes the corner values; a constant edge gives a bounded harmonic uuu that is discontinuous at two corners.

  • Factors: Table 33.1 in one direction, sinh⁡\sinhsinh or cosh⁡\coshcosh in the other.

Lecture 34 represents plane harmonic functions as real and imaginary parts of analytic functions and reads fields and flows from them.

References

Preparation: Lectures 2, 3 and 15 (harmonic functions), Lecture 29 (the heat and Poisson equations, superposition, the localization lemma, continuous functions on closed boxes, well-posed problems, Hadamard’s example), Lecture 31 (uniqueness from energy), Lecture 32 (the fixed-end eigenvalue problem, the theorem on sine series, termwise differentiation); GM 9, 29, 30 (mean value theorem, ratio test, uniform convergence), GM 37 (critical points, second-order Taylor formula), GM 40 (Green’s theorem), GM 42 (the outward normal derivative).

Reading: L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., §2.2.3 (the maximum principle) and §2.2.5 (energy methods); T. Myint-U and L. Debnath, Linear Partial Differential Equations for Scientists and Engineers, 4th ed., §§9.1–9.3, 9.7 and 9.9 (uniqueness, the Dirichlet and Neumann problems for a rectangle).
